sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Many of the most valuable companies are graphs
sections.para: Google, Facebook, LinkedIn, Amazon, Visa and Mastercard are graphs at heart, and four of them are among the ten most valuable companies. Ontologies are a business too. Graphs make answers obvious, but never scaled for everyone else because they were costly and built to lock in. Fractal semantic graphs change that.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Graph companies, and why graphs can scale now
sections.para: The biggest companies are graphs of links, people, products and payments; ontologies sell; everything from spreadsheets to law is a graph. With the right connections answers are obvious. Lock-in kept graphs for the few; shared-schema-free graphs and agents open them up.

sections.label: Graph companies
sections.para: Google's link graph and 2012 Knowledge Graph, Facebook's social graph of 69 billion friendships, LinkedIn's economic graph, Amazon's product graph and Visa's 257.5 billion transactions. Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta are worth about $12.8 trillion.

sections.label: Logistics is a graph
sections.line: Logistics is a graph that pays
sections.para: The graph tells a logistics company what to do at each moment. UPS said its ORION route optimisation would save about 100 million miles and 10 million gallons a year.

sections.label: Ontologies are a business
sections.line: Ontologies and taxonomies as a business
sections.para: Palantir sells its Ontology as a digital twin of the organisation and grew revenue 56% to $4.5 billion in 2025. LSEG's PermID, Neo4j's $200 million ARR and ServiceNow's data.world deal show the wider market.

sections.label: Everything is a graph
sections.para: A spreadsheet, a relational database and a language model's computation are graphs. Legal research has been a citation graph since 1873. Governments and businesses would be more efficient thinking in graphs.

sections.label: The answer becomes obvious
sections.line: With the right connections, the answer is obvious
sections.para: As in a whodunit, removing irrelevant nodes and keeping the right connections leaves one path. It is why search, feeds and logistics work.

sections.label: Why graphs never scaled
sections.line: Expensive, locked in, and the customer a commodity
sections.para: Building graphs needed heavy technology; owners used them to lock customers in and competitors out, without shared schemas or code; and key nodes were treated as commodities. Knowledge graph software was about a billion-dollar market while graph companies are worth trillions.

sections.label: Now they can scale
sections.line: Fractal graphs and agents let anyone build them
sections.para: Fractal semantic graphs need no shared schema, agents maintain graphs well, and open schemas such as schema.org and the EU's core vocabularies mean a graph need not be a moat. That is the founders' opportunity.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: A lens, a date, and estimates
sections.para: Graph company is a lens; these firms do more. Market values are from 19 October 2026. Graphs are not the only cause of their value. Market sizes and UPS's savings are estimates and claims.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A memo and the primary sources
sections.para: Dinis's memo of 19 October 2026, with company announcements, filings and papers from Google, Facebook, LinkedIn, Amazon, Visa, Palantir, UPS and others.
